context: a letter from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
Your letter gladdened me as your hand writing always does, though the account of your state is anything but gladsome   Thank Mrs Darwin very much for her part. This is just the place for my wife who gains ground rapidly, but loses it, or much of it, every now & then & is bloodless for a time. nevertheless, when weak, Neuralgia does not attack her here, as at Kew, & she walks several miles, & eats like a Trojan.

This is a wonderfully pretty place, especially the banks of the river. the moors are loathsome & the hills low broad rockless treeless & contemptible. I am studying the moraines all day long with as much enthusiasm as I am capable of after laying in bed till 9 eating heavy breakfasts & looking forward to dinner as the summum bonum of existence.

I am reading Lubbock very carefully, it is excellent; most excellent, so well written sagacious & discriminating. How well & wisely he treats C. Lewis’ blunder & hastyness & the errors of others too. The Savage chapters are tantalizing for their brevity & incompleteness. Why did you not mention Lyells apologetic pages in your letter—to me— I suppose because the subject was most distressing— reason enough, for so it is— I am not satisfied with his apology at all— it is not handsome at all, & from an old Prince of science to a young aspirant, is not liberal I think. I am not surprised at Lubbock having been riled up originally: but cannot alter my opinion of the note, 1. that the accusation is too broad & loose (exaggerated I fear), & 2. the latter paragraph is a bitter sarcasm though wholly unintentionally so I quite believe— Do consider it. he first accuses Lyell of extracting whole sentences without acknowlegdment & then attributes the denial of the robbery to a regretted inadvertence! i.e. Lyell first robs, then prearranges a fib to hide it, before he is accused mind you—& lastly when accused regrets his wilful uncalled for fib, as an inadvertence! by Jove if this is not a climax of villainy what is? all an ignorant bye-stander could say is, that his conscience is of a piece with his conduct. I am taking an ignorant byestanders view of the case— of course I know well that Lyells conduct has in justice no such interpretation.— I hope Lubbock will take no more notice of the affair, it is not worth it, & never was. worth anything beyond a mere assurance that he was first, though apparently second in the field.

I know a little of Tylors brother— he is an FGS. & FLS. that Edward Forbes’ big heart embraced. The family are gas fitters &c &c, hardware tradesmen most wealthy & respectable, once quakers if not now quakers. I never saw this author. I am so glad you like the book. it is to me the most interesting since your orchid work that I have read, & like it I can always dip back with gusto, & be refreshed.

I have read vol: 2 of Leckie (not vol 1 yet) & am extremely interested & instructed. The next holiday I get I must read Buckle, of which I have only read part of vol 2. I am also reading Tom Payne who I think has been pretty largely plundered by Grey & Colenso.

We have the Benthams here & my cousin Inglis Palgrave. I have not begun Giffords book regularly, but dipped here & there. it seems awfully conceited, vague & meagre of accurate topographical or scientific information, & very diffuse, but wonderfully clever as a literary composition. & no doubt full of valuable historical matter— he is a queer fellow, eccentric like all his Grandfather’s grandchildren; with brains enough for us all if he would put them to work systematically.

I had the most enjoyable dinner I ever sat down to out your home or perhaps Lubbocks at Frank Palgraves the other day, the guests being Jowett Maurice & Gifford.— Browning & Stanley came afterwards.

Can you afford to subscribe to the Palestine Exploration fund. I am deeply interested in the proper expenditure of the money & with Spottiswood Grove & some other good men I hope to see it well worked. I have given £3.3 (annually) for 3 years.

Herbert Spencer observations on umbellifer are utterly wrong—his reasoning partially right. How very odd, that the Antirrhinum case occurred to me as to you; I think that part of his reasoning, all or in great part wrong. he makes too little of Insect agency in shaping flowers, & of hereditary influence— too much of light air & unconquerable love of symmetry in the plant— still there is much in the line of argument. He sends me the proof sheets to comment on. I have not seen them since— he did not know that you had taken up the modifying effects of insect agency in impregnation   as a general law, that is.

I have not seen Nat Hist. Review which will not pay, is all but defunct I hear! & cannot go on beyond the year.

Oliver is working at African plants & his lectures

Ever yrs affec | J D Hooker

My Charlie has taken hooping cough at school, he returns on 19th. which puts all our arrangements out as we must keep him apart, which is difficult during Willys holidays.

You were a good man to write me so pleasant a letter from Yorkshire. I live such a life, I have never heard of Palestine Explo: Fund; as you are interested in it, I am sure it must be good, & not merely to map the Temple, so I will with pleasure subscribe 3 or 5 guineas (whichever you like) for the 3 years— But you must tell me to whom to send money.—

Lyells corrected pages came when I was extra miserable; I read them & threw them away & now to my surprise find that I have no clear recollection about them,—only a feeling that I was disgusted with everything in world—

I was glad to read your article on Glaciers &c in Yorkshire— you seem to have been struck with what most deeply impressed me at Glen Roy (wrong as I was on whole subject) viz. the marvellous manner in which every detail of surface of land had been preserved for enormous period— This makes me a little sceptical whether Ramsay, Jukes &c are not a little overdoing sub-äerial denudation. In same Reader there was a striking article on English & foreign men of science; & I think unjust to England, except in pure Physiology; in Biology Owen & R. Brown ought to save us, & in Geology we are most rich.—

It is curious how we are reading same books— we intend to read Leckie & certainly to reread Buckle, which latter I admired greatly before.— I am heartily glad you like Lubbock’s book so much.— It made me grieve his taking to Politicks, & though I grieve that he has lost his Election, yet I suppose now that he is once bitten he will never give up Politicks, & Science is done for. Many men can make fair M.P.s, & how few can work in Science like him.—

I have been reading a pamphlet by Verlot on variation of flowers, which seems to me very good, but I doubt whether it would be worth your reading. It was published originally in Journal d’Hort. & so perhaps you have seen it. It is very good plan this republishing separately for sake of foreigners buying, & I wish I had tried to get permission of Linn. Soc for my Climbing paper, but it is now too late.—

Do not forget that you have my paper on Hybridism by Max Wichura.

I hope you are returned to your work refreshed like a giant by your huge breakfasts— How unlucky you are about contagious complaints with your children.—

I keep very weak & had much sickness yesterday, but am stronger this morning—

Yours ever affect | C. Darwin

Can you remember how we ever first met; it was in Park St. but what brought us together?? I have been rereading a few old letters of yours, & my heart is very warm towards you.—
